egmo-2016-01.title: A monotone triple
egmo-2016-01.body:
Indices are taken modulo $n$. Let $\delta_k=x_{k+1}-x_k$. If $\delta_k\delta_{k+1}<0$ for every $k$, the signs of $\delta_1,\delta_2,\dots,\delta_n$ would alternate strictly around a cycle of odd length $n$, which is impossible. So some $j$ has $\delta_j\delta_{j+1}\ge0$.

- If both are $\ge0$: $x_j\le x_{j+1}\le x_{j+2}$, and since $x_{j+1}\ge0$,
$$\min_i(x_i^2+x_{i+1}^2)\le x_j^2+x_{j+1}^2\le2x_{j+1}^2\le2x_{j+1}x_{j+2}\le\max_k 2x_kx_{k+1}.$$
- If both are $\le0$: $x_j\ge x_{j+1}\ge x_{j+2}$, and similarly
$$\min_i(x_i^2+x_{i+1}^2)\le x_{j+1}^2+x_{j+2}^2\le2x_{j+1}^2\le2x_jx_{j+1}\le\max_k2x_kx_{k+1}.$$
∎

egmo-2016-02.title: Two inverse similarities
egmo-2016-02.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ between lines, modulo $180^\circ$. Since $E\ne F$, the point $X$ is not on line $MY$, so $E,F,X$ are not collinear. By the tangent–chord theorem, $XY$ is tangent to circle $EFX$ iff
$$\measuredangle(XY,XE)=\measuredangle(FX,FE),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \measuredangle(XY,AC)=\measuredangle(BD,YM).$$
Splitting at $Y$, $A$ and $B$:
$$\measuredangle(XY,AC)=\measuredangle(YX,YA)+\measuredangle(AY,AX),\qquad \measuredangle(BD,YM)=\measuredangle(BX,BY)+\measuredangle(YB,YM).$$
We prove the two parts match.

**Part 1: $\measuredangle(AY,AX)=\measuredangle(BX,BY)$.** Since $XA\cdot XC=XB\cdot XD$ and $\angle AXD=\angle BXC$, there is an orientation-reversing similarity $\sigma'$ fixing $X$ with $A\mapsto B$, $D\mapsto C$. It maps the midpoint $D_1$ of $XD$ to the midpoint $C_1$ of $XC$. So it maps lines $AX$, $AD_1$ to $BX$, $BC_1$. Orientation reversal negates directed angles:
$$\measuredangle(BX,BY)=\measuredangle(BX,BC_1)=-\measuredangle(AX,AD_1)=\measuredangle(AY,AX).$$

**Part 2: $\measuredangle(YX,YA)=\measuredangle(YB,YM)$.**
- *$A,B,C_1,D_1$ are concyclic.* $XA\cdot XC_1=\tfrac12XA\cdot XC=\tfrac12XB\cdot XD=XB\cdot XD_1$, with $X$ between $A$ and $C_1$ and between $B$ and $D_1$.
- *An inverse similarity at $Y$.* The point $Y$ lies on lines $AD_1$ and $BC_1$. By the power of the point $Y$, triangles $YAB$ and $YC_1D_1$ are inversely similar: there is an orientation-reversing similarity $\sigma$ fixing $Y$ with $A\mapsto C_1$, $B\mapsto D_1$.
- *$\sigma(X)=M$.* By the midline theorem in triangle $XCD$: $C_1D_1\parallel CD$, $C_1M\parallel XD=BD$, $D_1M\parallel XC=AC$. The line $\sigma(AX)$ passes through $C_1$ and satisfies
$$\measuredangle(C_1D_1,\sigma(AX))=-\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle(AC,AB)=\measuredangle(DC,DB)=\measuredangle(C_1D_1,C_1M),$$
using the inscribed angle theorem for $ABCD$. So $\sigma(AX)=C_1M$. Similarly,
$$\measuredangle(D_1C_1,\sigma(BX))=-\measuredangle(BA,BD)=\measuredangle(BD,BA)=\measuredangle(CD,CA)=\measuredangle(D_1C_1,D_1M),$$
so $\sigma(BX)=D_1M$. Hence $\sigma(X)=C_1M\cap D_1M=M$.

Since $\sigma$ fixes $Y$ and reverses angles,
$$\measuredangle(YC_1,YM)=-\measuredangle(YA,YX)=\measuredangle(YX,YA),$$
and $YC_1$ is the line $YB$. This proves Part 2.

Adding Parts 1 and 2 gives $\measuredangle(XY,AC)=\measuredangle(BD,YM)$, so $XY$ is tangent to the circle $EFX$ at $X$. ∎

egmo-2016-03.title: Construction and a bipartite graph
egmo-2016-03.body:
**Answer: $6m$.**

**Construction.** Divide the array into $4\times4$ blocks and use the $m$ blocks on the main diagonal. In each, colour the cells $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3)$ and $(2,4),(3,4),(4,4)$ (local coordinates), i.e. three cells in the first row and three cells in the last column, $6m$ cells in total.
- Inside a diagonal block: a cell of row $1$ sees at least two other blue cells in row $1$. A cell of column $4$ in rows $2$–$4$ sees the other two blue cells of column $4$. A cell $(i,j)$ with $i\ge2$, $j\le3$ sees $(i,4)$ in its row and $(1,j)$ in its column.
- Outside the diagonal blocks: every row and every column of the array contains at least one blue cell (each diagonal block has a blue cell in each of its rows and columns). A cell outside the diagonal blocks is not blue, and its row and column each contain a blue cell, giving two.

**Lower bound.** Form a bipartite graph whose $8m$ vertices are the rows and the columns; join row $r$ to column $c$ when cell $(r,c)$ is blue. The blue cells are the edges. Cell $(r,c)$ is related to $\deg r+\deg c-2[\,(r,c)\text{ blue}\,]$ blue cells.
- If some row is empty, then every cell $(r,c)$ in it needs $\deg c\ge2$ for all $4m$ columns, giving at least $8m>6m$ blue cells. The same holds for an empty column. So assume there are no isolated vertices.
- Take any edge $rc$. The condition at cell $(r,c)$ gives $\deg r+\deg c\ge4$. So the component of $rc$ contains $r$, $c$ and at least $(\deg r-1)+(\deg c-1)\ge2$ further vertices: **every component has at least $4$ vertices.** Hence there are at most $8m/4=2m$ components.
- A connected graph on $v$ vertices has at least $v-1$ edges. So the number of edges is at least $8m-(\text{number of components})\ge8m-2m=6m$.

So at least $6m$ blue cells are needed, and $6m$ suffice.

egmo-2016-04.title: Two homotheties
egmo-2016-04.body:
Let $O_1,O_2,O$ be the centres, $R$ the common radius of $\omega_1,\omega_2$ and $r$ the radius of $\omega$. We treat points as vectors.

**Symmetry of the two equal circles.** Let $N$ be the midpoint of $O_1O_2$. The point reflection in $N$ swaps $O_1$ and $O_2$, hence swaps $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, and maps the set $\{X_1,X_2\}$ to itself. It does not fix $X_1$, since $N$ lies strictly inside both circles (they meet in two points). So it swaps $X_1$ and $X_2$. Hence $X_2=2N-X_1$ and $O_2=2N-O_1$, so
$$X_2-O_2=-(X_1-O_1).$$

**The homotheties.** The homothety $h_1$ with centre $T_1$ and ratio $-r/R$ maps $\omega_1$ to $\omega$ (external tangency). The homothety $h_2$ with centre $T_2$ and ratio $+r/R$ maps $\omega_2$ to $\omega$ (internal tangency). A homothety with ratio $k$ maps $O_i\mapsto O$ and multiplies vectors by $k$, so
$$h_1(X_1)-O=-\tfrac rR(X_1-O_1)=\tfrac rR(X_2-O_2)=h_2(X_2)-O .$$
So $Z=h_1(X_1)=h_2(X_2)$ is a single point of $\omega$. A homothety moves points along lines through its centre, so $Z$ lies on line $T_1X_1$ and on line $T_2X_2$.

Hence the lines $X_1T_1$ and $X_2T_2$ meet at $Z$, which lies on $\omega$. ∎

egmo-2016-05.title: Empty rows are consecutive
egmo-2016-05.body:
Use coordinates on the board $[0,n]\times[0,n]$. A row *contains a tile* if a horizontal tile lies in it; similarly for columns and vertical tiles.

**Case $n=k$.** Every tile spans a full row or a full column. A horizontal and a vertical tile would cross, so all tiles have the same direction, say horizontal. Maximality then puts a tile in every row, giving exactly $n$ tiles. **Minimum $n$.**

From now on $k<n<2k$.

**Constructions.**
- *$k<n\le2k-2$, with $2n-2k+2$ tiles.* Place the horizontal tiles $[0,k]\times[0,1]$, $[1,k+1]\times[k,k+1]$ and the vertical tiles $[0,1]\times[1,k+1]$, $[k,k+1]\times[0,k]$ (a pinwheel around an empty $(k-1)\times(k-1)$ square). Add $n-k-1$ horizontal tiles stacked in $[1,k+1]\times[k+1,n]$ and $n-k-1$ vertical tiles in $[k+1,n]\times[1,k+1]$. The empty regions are a $(k-1)\times(k-1)$ square, two $1\times(n-k-1)$ strips and an $(n-k-1)\times(n-k-1)$ square, all with sides $<k$. So no tile fits.
- *$n=2k-1$, with $n$ tiles.* Stack $k-1$ horizontal tiles in $[0,k]\times[0,k-1]$, another $k-1$ in $[0,k]\times[k,2k-1]$, and add $[k-1,2k-1]\times[k-1,k]$. The empty regions are two $(k-1)\times(k-1)$ squares and a $(k-1)\times1$ strip, so the arrangement is maximal.

Since $2n-2k+2\le n$ iff $n\le2k-2$, these use $\min(n,2n-2k+2)$ tiles.

**Lower bound.** Take a maximal arrangement. Let $r$ be the number of rows and $c$ the number of columns not containing a tile.

*Claim: the rows not containing a tile are consecutive.* Let a horizontal tile $T$ lie in row $\rho$ and columns $a+1,\dots,a+k$. Since $(\rho-1)+(n-\rho)=n-1\le2k-2$, one side of row $\rho$, say rows $1,\dots,\rho-1$, has at most $k-1$ rows. In the rectangle formed by these rows and $T$'s columns:
- no vertical tile can meet it: such a tile could not pass row $\rho$ (occupied by $T$) and would have to fit in fewer than $k$ rows;
- so if one of these rows contained no horizontal tile, its $k$ cells above $T$ would be empty, and a tile could be added there.

Hence every row between $T$ and that edge of the board contains a tile. If tile-free rows $i<l$ had a tile-containing row $j$ between them, applying this to a tile in row $j$ would force row $i$ or row $l$ to contain a tile. Contradiction. The same holds for columns.

- If $r=0$ or $c=0$, every row (or column) contains its own tile, so there are at least $n$ tiles.
- If $r,c>0$, the $r$ tile-free rows and $c$ tile-free columns are consecutive, so they cross in an $r\times c$ rectangle of empty cells (any tile covering such a cell would lie in that row or column). By maximality $r\le k-1$ and $c\le k-1$. So at least $n-k+1$ rows contain a horizontal tile and at least $n-k+1$ columns contain a vertical tile, giving at least $2n-2k+2$ tiles.

Either way there are at least $\min(n,2n-2k+2)$ tiles.

**Answer:** the minimum is $n$ when $n=k$, and $\min(n,2n-2k+2)$ when $k<n\le2k-1$.

egmo-2016-06.title: Reduce to Pell equations
egmo-2016-06.body:
**Lemma.** $n\in S$ iff $2n^2+1$ or $12n^2+9$ is a perfect square.

*Proof.* Let $d=n^2+k$ divide $n^4$ with $1\le k\le2n$. From $n^2\equiv-k\pmod d$ we get $d\mid n^4-k^2$, so $d\mid k^2$; let $k^2=qd$. As $n^2<d<(n+1)^2$, $d$ is not a square, so $q\ne1$. Also $q=\frac{k^2}{n^2+k}\le\frac{4n^2}{n^2+1}<4$. So $q\in\{2,3\}$.
- $q=2$: $k^2=2n^2+2k$ gives $2n^2+1=(k-1)^2$.
- $q=3$: $k^2=3n^2+3k$ gives $12n^2+9=(2k-3)^2$.

Conversely:
- If $2n^2+1=t^2$, then $t<2n$ and $n^4=(n^2+1)^2-t^2=(n^2+t+1)(n^2-t+1)$. So $n^2+t+1$ is a divisor in the range, as $t+1\le2n$.
- If $12n^2+9=t^2$, then $t$ is odd and $n^4=(n^2+\tfrac32)^2-\tfrac{t^2}{4}$, so $n^2+\frac{t+3}{2}$ divides $n^4$. Moreover $3\mid t$ and $3\mid n$ (see below), so $n\ge6$, and then $t\le4n-3$ (equivalent to $4n^2\ge24n$). Hence $\frac{t+3}2\le2n$. $\square$

**First family.** $t^2-2n^2=1$ is a Pell equation with fundamental solution $(3,2)$. All its positive solutions are $(t_j,n_j)$ with $(t_0,n_0)=(1,0)$ and $(t_{j+1},n_{j+1})=(3t_j+4n_j,\,2t_j+3n_j)$. Modulo $7$:
$$(1,0)\to(3,2)\to(3,5)\to(1,0).$$
The sequence is generated by a fixed linear map, so it is periodic mod $7$ with period $3$. The values $n_j$ run through $2,-2,0$ repeatedly: infinitely many $n\in S$ with $n\equiv0,\pm2\pmod7$.

**Second family.** If $t^2=12n^2+9$, then $3\mid t^2$, so $t=3t'$ and $t'^2=\frac{4n^2}{3}+1$. Hence $3\mid n$; with $n=3n'$, this is $t'^2-12n'^2=1$, with fundamental solution $(7,2)$. Its solutions give $(t,n)=(3t',3n')$, starting $(21,6)$ and following $(t,n)\mapsto(7t+24n,\,2t+7n)$. Modulo $7$:
$$(0,-1)\to(-3,0)\to(0,1)\to(3,0)\to(0,-1),$$
with period $4$. So $n$ runs through $-1,0,1,0$: infinitely many $n\in S$ with $n\equiv0,\pm1\pmod7$.

**Conclusion.** By the lemma, $S$ consists exactly of the $n$-values of these two families (Pell solutions are exactly the powers of the fundamental solution). Their residues mod $7$ are only $0,\pm1,\pm2$, each occurring infinitely often. So $S$ has infinitely many elements $\equiv0,1,2,5,6\pmod7$ and none $\equiv3,4\pmod7$. ∎
